papers.title: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology
papers.summary: Connectome-constrained models are often used to argue that a measured wiring diagram outperforms shuffled or rewired wiring, and hence that structure shapes function. Such comparisons can confound wiring with how the models are tuned: a connectome fixes who connects to whom, not the excitability, gains or plasticity rates the model also needs, and modellers often tune these until the real-wiring model works. We separate three estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 restricted to physiology consistent with independent data (P3). The biases involved are known in machine learning (under-tuned baselines, inherited weights, winner's curse); we measure what they do to biological conclusions, using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models. Some claims survive every protocol we test: segregated reward and punishment dopamine improves learning, and head-direction topography is required for a persistent bump. Others do not. In the mushroom body, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 under P1 and P2 but loses to it by 0.09 under P3 (95% CIs exclude zero; held-out runs confirm). The verdict is set by the share of alpha'beta' cells among active Kenyon cells, which P1 selects low; at the share implied by imaging (about 44%) the real-wiring model fails to learn, exposing a model inadequacy rather than a deficit of the fly's wiring. In flyvis, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome, which has a constructed solution within 0.07 (median) of the real error, more than a spatially shuffled one in 50 of 50 members; the ranking survives ten-fold longer retraining but depends on the checkpoint at fifty-fold. A credible structural claim needs matched optimisation, data-constrained physiology and a model that still works there.
papers.comment: 23 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables. Code, data and prediction files are included as ancillary files

papers.title: Measuring Robustness and Efficiency in a Connectome-Constrained Fly Visual System Model: Linking an Adversarial and a Perceptual Illusion
papers.summary: Biological visual systems compute reliably under tight metabolic and wiring constraints, whereas artificial vision systems consume far more energy and can be sensitive to adversarial perturbations. Whether networks with brain-like wiring are more robust at lower computational cost is unclear. We address this by benchmarking a task-optimized, continuous-time recurrent neural network of the fly visual system constrained by its synaptic connectome (FlyNet) against artificial neural networks. We compare it against CNNs, RAFT, and continuous-time recurrent neural networks without detailed connectome constraints (sCTRNN, CTRNN) on a collision-detection task within a differentiable 3D rendering pipeline. FlyNet is adversarially vulnerable but, relative to its compute, more robust to common video corruptions than RAFT, while using up to five orders of magnitude fewer FLOPs. The CTRNNs remain more robust than FlyNet across almost all tested perturbations, suggesting that connectome constraints benefit efficiency, through their low edge count, over robustness. Recurrence improves robustness to white-box attacks in RAFT and temporal context improves robustness to common corruptions. FlyNet's position and velocity representations degrade under adversarial textures but recover under counterfactual textures that restore correct classification while staying equally far from training, ruling out unfamiliar textures as the cause of failure. The reverse-phi illusion similarly disrupts these representations and inverts the same low-level motion statistic as the adversarial textures. Optimizing this input statistic alone, without access to the network, suffices to induce classification failure, attributing both perturbations to the same circuit vulnerability. Connectome-constrained models can thus surface adversarial failure mechanisms as testable hypotheses about biological perceptual vulnerabilities.

papers.title: Optimization principles, revisited
papers.summary: The brain solves a wide range of problems, and some of these solutions are very good indeed. It is an old idea that, in some cases, these solutions may be as good as possible given the relevant constraints. If this is true we can promote this notion of optimization to a principle from which aspects of function and mechanism can be derived, ideally with no free parameters. Optimization principles are powerful and have had many successes, but they remain controversial. We start with a reminder of a classic example---diffraction limited optics in insect eyes---and then a summary of why you should worry about optimization as a more general principle. Next we turn to recent progress on the theory of optimal motion estimation in fly vision, and finally summarize recent results on the landscape for optimization, arguing that (contrary to widely held intuitions) optimal performance need not require the underlying mechanisms to have finely tuned parameters. I hope to convince you that this is a moment to take optimization seriously as the basis for theories of neural coding and computation. This is based on a rather informal lecture at the summer school LASCON X in Sao Paulo, and I have tried to preserve that tone here; pointers are given to more detailed and technical discussions.
papers.comment: Based on a lecture at LASCON X, https://sisne.org/en/lascon-x/

papers.title: ScaleBrain: A Scale-Consistent Framework for EEG Foundation Models
papers.summary: Foundation models pre-trained on large unlabeled electroencephalography (EEG) corpora have emerged as a transformative paradigm for Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) applications. Recent EEG foundation models have shown that multi-scale representations derived from fixed-length patches can improve EEG representation learning. Existing frameworks commonly construct temporal scales through feature-level operations. However, these operations leave the correspondence between learned features and scale-specific characteristics of the original EEG signals implicit. Moreover, when the self-supervised objective is not aligned with the multi-scale input representations, information at some temporal scales may receive insufficient supervision during pre-training. In light of this, we propose ScaleBrain, a scale-consistent pre-training framework that explicitly coordinates multi-scale representations of EEG from both the model input and optimization objective sides. Specifically, ScaleBrain introduces multi-scale EEG tokenization to represent the same EEG segment through analysis windows with different temporal spans and shared temporal anchors, and pairs these representations with scale-specific reconstruction to align with the multi-scale input structure and provide supervision across temporal resolutions during self-supervised learning. We further develop an axial spatio-temporal attention mechanism to contextualize the fused multi-scale representation along spatial and temporal dimensions. Extensive evaluations on six public BCI benchmarks against 12 representative baselines show that ScaleBrain achieves the highest mean Balanced Accuracy on five datasets and ranks third on the remaining one, with only 5.0M parameters, demonstrating strong performance and favorable parameter efficiency.

papers.title: Neuromodulation Through Intrinsic Noise
papers.summary: Neuromodulation, the modulation of excitability through the regulation of neuronal parameters, is a key tool in neuromorphic control design. This paper investigates how spiking excitability can be modulated by intrinsic noise. Focusing on a simplified memristive neuron model, we show that intrinsic noise plays distinct functional roles depending on the feedback pathways: Intrinsic noise in the fast excitatory feedback shapes the nature of excitability and modulates the sensitivity of the neuron to external/internal stimuli, whereas that in the slow inhibitory feedback provides internal stimuli that can trigger stochastic spiking. We expect these findings to guide the design of neuromorphic systems that harness intrinsic noise to exploit beneficial stochastic phenomena, such as stochastic resonance.
category_names_zh: eess.SY (系统与控制理论 (Systems and Control))

papers.title: Similar visual tuning conceals different recovery dynamics in a model of macaque V1
papers.summary: Biologically detailed neuronal networks can model how brain circuits perform observed functions, but their high computational cost limits the comparisons needed to test biological hypotheses. To address this limitation, we extend a multiscale approach in which responses of small populations of spiking neurons are computed in advance and reused across a larger cortical circuit. In particular, we approximate these local responses by deep neural networks and achieve an estimated acceleration of the order $10^5$ for steady-state evaluation relative to spiking network simulation. Beyond computational acceleration, the smooth deep surrogate of local responses provides derivatives, allowing us to analyze linear stability and to trace how a perturbation in brain activity is transmitted through different pathways. We demonstrate the approach in a model of an input layer of macaque primary visual cortex (V1), testing circuits under visual stimulation and controlled perturbations. We resolve pathway contributions to stability, strong recurrent responses, and slow recovery. Yet different combinations of pathway strengths can support similar responses to visual stimuli while producing different recovery dynamics. Therefore, Steady responses and perturbation recovery place complementary constraints on candidate circuits. Overall, our approach offers efficient evaluation with an interpretable circuit structure, making systematic comparisons across stimuli and biological hypotheses practical.

papers.title: A Functional Preservation Score for Auditing Connectome Operations: Compression, Alignment, Transport, and Local-Rule Writing
papers.summary: We introduce the Functional Preservation Score (FPS), a null-normalised, behaviourally grounded measure of how much of a neural network's input-output function survives a structural operation, and use it to audit the operations underlying speculative "mind-migration" pipelines on public data that runs on a single laptop. Across five pre-registered studies on the C. elegans connectome, whole-brain calcium activity, and hippocampal replay, FPS yields two positive characterisations and a three-part negative. Low-bit quantisation of a real connectome exhibits a structure-dependent sparsity floor: uniform int4/ternary quantisation is forced to roughly 73%/98% effective sparsity because heavy-tailed integer synaptic weights round to zero, while mixed-precision protection of hub neurons lowers these floors to about 27%/32%. Decoded hippocampal replay sequences compress heavily yet remain identifiable at a cross-validated top-1 accuracy of 0.69 (95% CI [0.63, 0.74]; chance 0.125; permutation p < 1e-3) from latents of order 10-50 bits per event, and a bounded incremental store shows a graceful-versus-cliff capacity trade-off. The migration pipeline fails in simulation at each stage for largely independent reasons: the putative "identity payload" is not a functionally separable module (p >= 0.16 at every tested size); cross-individual functional transport via Gromov-Wasserstein collapses once the target's wiring is respected (fidelity 1.00 to 0.40, [0.31, 0.49], p < 1e-3) or alignment is imperfect (0.06, [0.00, 0.13]); and biologically plausible local plasticity cannot reach the function the target topology provably admits (gap 0.45, [0.27, 0.64], p < 1e-3, d = 2.0). We release FPS, the data loaders, and all operations as a toolkit. All results are at nematode / small-network scale and concern coherence in simulation, not the feasibility of reading or writing a living brain.
papers.comment: 5 pages, 4 figures. Code, data loaders, and all result artifacts at https://github.com/Praveg432/functional-preservation-score

papers.title: Human and Machine Annotations Predict Brain Responses to Naturalistic Movies Across Development
papers.summary: Naturalistic movie watching provides a powerful framework for studying dynamic brain function, but linking movie content to neural responses typically relies on labor-intensive human annotation. We investigated whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can provide scalable socio-affective and semantic annotations for naturalistic fMRI. We compared MLLM-generated theory-of-mind (ToM) and valence ratings with human ratings and with regional BOLD responses across three animated movies. For two of these movies, we combined machine-derived visual features, natural-language scene descriptions, and socio-affective ratings in an ROI-wise encoding model of fMRI data from 66 participants aged 5--22 years. MLLM ratings partially tracked human judgments, but their neural correspondence differed by construct and model: ToM showed the most consistent human--machine overlap in visual cortex, whereas valence correspondence was largely movie dependent. In the encoding model, visual features yielded the strongest and most widespread prediction, whereas scene descriptions were more spatially selective, concentrated in dorsal-attention and visual regions and extending into right lateral temporal cortex. Age-group comparisons suggested feature-specific developmental differences: scene-description encoding in dorsal-attention cortex was higher in the oldest group, whereas visual-feature encoding in salience/ventral-attention, limbic, and control networks peaked in the middle group. Together, these findings indicate that MLLM-generated annotations capture meaningful aspects of human judgments and neural responses, supporting MLLMs as a scalable complement to, rather than a replacement for, human annotation in naturalistic neuroimaging.

papers.title: Lightweight Deep Learning Framework for Astrocyte-Centric 3D Reconstruction across Normal and Stress-associated Ultrastructural States
papers.summary: The morphology of astrocytes is closely associated with their ability to support and modulate neural circuit functions; however, its reconstruction from volume electron microscopy (vEM) data remains labor-intensive and computationally resource-intensive, placing substantial barriers on its broader adoption and scalability despite the high spatial resolution of vEM. We present AstroSeg-vEM, a lightweight, astrocyte-centric framework for morphology-preserving astrocyte segmentation, 3D reconstruction, and quantitative morphological analysis in vEM images. AstroSeg-vEM combines transformer-based 2D segmentation with dedicated post-processing methods and operates directly on high-resolution EM sections, making it well suited to anisotropic vEM data and downstream proofreading workflows while preserving the full in-plane resolution of the original EM data. Across four mouse hippocampal datasets representing normal and morphologically defined stress-associated astrocyte ultrastructural states, AstroSeg-vEM demonstrates robust performance and generalization, achieving average Dice and weighted Dice values of 0.92 and 0.95, respectively, on a held-out test dataset. Its lightweight architecture enables efficient, high-fidelity reconstruction on consumer-grade hardware, providing a scalable and accessible platform for large-scale astrocyte ultrastructure analysis and future astrocyte-neuron interaction studies.

papers.title: Orthographic depth at two scales, with English also matched for lexicon size
papers.summary: A reader can struggle to read in only one of their languages, and one proposed reason is how predictably spelling maps to sound. We measure that predictability as conditional entropy, the pronunciation uncertainty left once the spelling is seen, at two grain sizes (unit sizes): the alignment unit, an aligned spelling-sound chunk, and the syllable, bounded in the pronunciation. We analyse word lists in twelve alphabetic orthographies and report five in full, with English pronunciations from a dictionary and the rest from the synthesizer eSpeak-ng, length marks removed. Among the five, English has the most uncertainty and Finnish the least at both grains. Across all twelve, Portuguese and Danish exceed English per alignment unit, and German and Italian order differently by grain and transcription. These orders hold when English is transcribed by eSpeak-ng with u allowed to spell /j/ plus a vowel. Uncertainty per unit has no shared direction as units grow: it falls in Spanish and, less securely, German, is level in Finnish, depends on transcription in Italian and on the word list in English, and rises in Norwegian and Swedish. Summed uncertainty per word falls in all twelve, but that score is handed the pronunciation's boundaries and mixes context with in-sample memorisation, so it is no evidence of what a reader computes. An exact identity states when discarded spelling boundaries could reverse that fall. A uniform 20,000-word English sample holds 35% of the dictionary's syllable spellings and has syllable entropy 0.098 bits lower, so lexicons must be matched in size. In an exploratory check over eleven languages, syllable-scale entropy tracked first-year reading accuracy (rho = -0.74, falling to -0.25 if English is given the lowest entropy instead), without separating the syllable scale from the alignment unit. These estimates describe sampled writing systems, not readers.

papers.title: A probabilistic model of visual segmentation explains early visual cortical dynamics
papers.summary: Neural dynamics are a central feature of biological neural systems. In the visual cortex, the functional role of neural dynamics is poorly understood, particularly for static stimuli. The statistics of still natural images have long been used by models that successfully predict firing in early visual cortex; those models assume that neurons represent inferences about latent image features, but often ignore the dynamics of said inference. Here, we test if inferential dynamics in images explain visual-cortical dynamics. To do so, we present a biologically plausible model of cortical computation which assumes that the inference of features is coupled with inference about how those features are organized into meaningful parts, a function also known as segmentation. Given an input image, our model iterates between inferring the features and the segments, through recurrence and feedback, thus inducing dynamics in the neural representation of features. For these neural dynamics, we derive theoretical and exact predictions. Our model predicts both gain and variability in evoked responses to natural images, and we show that it captures classical single-neuron experimental findings such as gain dynamics and variability decay during stimulus presentation. The model also predicts that those dynamics are organized around inferred segment structure and more heterogeneous than previously thought, reflecting the complexity of inference for natural scenes. Finally, our analytical formulation provides a clear interpretation of our results. Insights from our normative model could generalize to segmentation problems in other experimental modalities, and help address the cost of inference in artificial networks with iterative computation.

papers.title: IC-GNN: Modeling Individualized Brain Community Organization for Disease Prediction
papers.summary: Brain networks exhibit modular organization, where community structures vary substantially across individuals and diseases. Understanding these individual differences is crucial for advancing both basic neuroscience research and precision medicine. However, widely used predefined group-level brain atlases often overlook this heterogeneity. While individualized functional parcellations capture subject-specific variability in community boundaries, they often require lengthy scan times to achieve fine-grained resolution and complicate cross-subject comparisons. To address this trade-off and investigate how individualized community organization captures disease-associated changes across individuals, we propose IC-GNN, an atlas-anchored model that forms distinct, individualized functional communities directly over atlas-defined brain regions. IC-GNN derives discrete, individualized multiscale communities from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, refines community-guided connections, and adapts shared regional weights to each subject's community context to enable both individualized modeling and group-level comparisons. Across more than 30,000 participants from ABIDE (autism spectrum disorder), ADNI (Alzheimer's disease), and the UK Biobank (depression), IC-GNN achieves the highest performance compared with 15 baseline methods. We further demonstrate that these individualized communities are reproducible within scans and across sessions, and carry predictive power on their own. Furthermore, IC-GNN identifies disease-related shifts in community organization that align with established literature, highlighting a promising approach for modeling individualized community structure for disease prediction and biomarker discovery.

papers.title: Qualiaphobic artificial neural networks (and why to build them)
papers.summary: This paper introduces qualiaphobic AI: artificial neural network architectures that are hostile to theories of consciousness. I show that qualiaphobia can be well-justified by knowledge about theories of consciousness, like when such theories are trivial or unfalsifiable or contradicted by overwhelming scientific evidence. It can also be justified by how theories of consciousness must be grounded in phenomenology, as well as how current popular theories of consciousness are applied to AI. I identify and explore three convergent ways of engineering qualiaphobia that would minimize the potential for artificial consciousness. These include making AI architectures as close as possible to "anchor points" of systems with minimal potential for consciousness, fragmenting any potential phenomenology AI might have, and designing artificial neural networks in a way adversarial to popular theories of consciousness. In particular, I develop one "anchor point" of minimal potential for consciousness: systems where only behaviorist theories of consciousness can apply, and I propose qualiaphobic transformations that move existing artificial neural networks toward such systems. Additionally, I develop an account of how AIs can form justified beliefs about their own non-consciousness (or minimal potential for consciousness) and expand on how this knowledge would change their behavior. Most critically, I begin with why this research is important: qualiaphobic AI has epistemic properties that make it far better aligned with human civilization. Since consciousness is central to moral value, a world in which AIs are non-conscious ensures it is always morally correct for AI to assist and serve humanity, rather than pursue its own ends.

papers.title: Spike-to-Field Mechanisms of Turbulence-Like Dynamics in Spatial Spiking Neural Networks
papers.summary: Neural avalanches and turbulence-like brain dynamics are usually measured after neural activity has been coarse-grained into continuous fields, leaving open which spike-level mechanisms can generate these macroscopic observables. We build a spatial leaky integrate-and-fire spiking neural network and explicitly transform spikes into activity-density and Hilbert phase fields. A delayed, distance-dependent, passive-dendrite regime reproducibly generates turbulence-like field structure, including high-amplitude phase-defect tracks, structure-function scaling, and power-law-favored continuous-field avalanche tails. Controls show that firing rate, vortex count, and avalanche tail fits are individually insufficient: destroying delayed propagation, dendritic filtering, or spike timing suppresses key field signatures, while random-space nulls can retain many mathematical phase defects but show weaker spatial structure and synaptic-delay transfer. Biologically motivated gates further shape the regime: PV-like perisomatic inhibition clamps phase dynamics, SST-like dendritic inhibition and projection-specific inhibitory facilitation preserve long-lived tracks, and a rate-constrained projection-STP regime expresses a roughly 200-ms episode at 12.25 Hz (full-record mean) across 12 seeds. These results use SNNs as a mechanistic testbed for spike-derived brain turbulence observables and show why phase defects and avalanche-like statistics must be interpreted jointly with spatial scaling and spike-level propagation.
papers.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 23 pages, including references, appendices, and checklist

papers.title: K-prop: Deep Online Learning by Backpropagating Temporal Kernels
papers.summary: Self-recurrence represents an important component for temporal processing in neural networks, both artificial and biological, where it appears naturally in the form of leaky integration. However, due to the complex temporal dependencies of the gradient, an efficient and effective method of online training is still lacking. Here we propose K-prop, a novel online learning method for leaky neural networks. It dramatically reduces the computational and memory cost of real time recurrent learning (RTRL) by propagating kernel gains. K-prop also outperforms existing RTRL approximations and achieves performance comparable to backpropagation through time in sequence learning, classification, and reinforcement learning tasks. We further analyze how its sole approximation affects gradient quality and identify conditions under which K-prop remains accurate and effective.
papers.comment: Accepted for publication in Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 40 (NeurIPS 2026)

papers.title: TrajLift: Lifting Memory Recall Trajectories with Latency-Modulated Heat Diffusion
papers.summary: Verbal memory retrieval carries rich diagnostic information for Alzheimer's disease through the order, hesitation, and categorical organization of recalled words, yet computational modeling of this retrieval process remains largely unexplored. A key challenge is that timing and hierarchical structure are diagnostically entangled: the diagnostic meaning of retrieval timing depends on its hierarchical context. We propose TrajLift, a spectral framework that models verbal recall as timed trajectories on a hierarchical graph. Our central mechanism is latency-modulated heat diffusion on the semantic hierarchy, a unified operator that lifts each recalled word into a representation of both multi-scale hierarchical structure and continuous retrieval timing. Formal analysis shows that the resulting representation is first-order separable into structural and temporal components with spectral selectivity across hierarchical levels. On synthetic benchmarks requiring structure-time interaction, TrajLift stays near-perfect on deep hierarchies where all baselines fail. On real-world clinical data, we show that TrajLift outperforms diverse baselines by jointly modeling timing and semantic structure, with gains that grow as retrieval timing becomes more informative.
category_names_zh: cs.CL (计算语言与大语言模型 (NLP))

papers.title: Language processing in the autistic brain: A meta-analysis of neuroimaging studies across modalities and age
papers.summary: Language is central to social communication, which is altered in autism, and language abilities vary widely among autistic individuals. How the autistic brain processes language is central to understanding autistic communication. Yet neuroimaging studies report inconsistent findings on how autistic brain activity is altered during language processing. We synthesized 45 fMRI and PET studies (753 autistic and 777 non-autistic participants) with seed-based d mapping with permutation of subject images (SDM-PSI). We estimated autistic and non-autistic activation and their difference with meta-regressions adjusted for each study's language modality and mean age. Autistic and non-autistic brains activated a similar left-lateralized language network. Autistic brains showed reduced activity throughout the left perisylvian cortex, from the inferior frontal gyrus to the mid superior temporal gyrus and the posterior superior temporal sulcus, and increased activity in the right temporal pole. Spoken language showed a larger autistic reduction than written language in the left mid superior temporal gyrus. Adults, but not children and adolescents, showed increased autistic activity in the right superior temporal gyrus and cuneus. Autistic language processing thus relies on the typical left-lateralized network but shows reduced leftward lateralization.
category_names_zh: cs.CL (计算语言与大语言模型 (NLP))

papers.title: MICE: Multi-animal Interaction Context Encoder - A Hierarchical Foundation Model for Mouse Behavior
papers.summary: Quantifying mouse behavior from pose is a foundational tool in neuroscience, ethology, drug discovery, and animal welfare. Self-supervised foundation models are a natural fit, but a foundation model for mouse behavior must handle social behavior - many behaviors that matter (aggression, courtship, mounting, allogrooming) are inherently multi-animal. Existing self-supervised pose models fall short: they encode each animal independently and discard interaction signal, hard-code the animal count, and pretrain one dataset at a time. We introduce MICE (Multi-animal Interaction Context Encoder), a hierarchical foundation model for mouse behavior that pretrains jointly on six mouse-pose corpora spanning one to four mice and 7 to 27 keypoints. MICE combines a hierarchical individual encoder capturing per-mouse kinematics at multiple temporal scales with a Perceiver-style social encoder whose learned latent codebook decouples parameter count from animal count, so a single checkpoint serves any group size without retraining. Across four evaluation protocols spanning six datasets, MICE matches or exceeds prior keypoint-based baselines, and layer-wise probing shows the social stage incrementally improves discriminability beyond the individual encoder. Code, weights, and data are available at https://github.com/eric0708/MICE.
category_names_zh: cs.CV (计算机视觉与模式识别 (CV))

papers.title: From MNH to the Friedman--Komogortsev Method---which changes improve eye-movement classification?
papers.summary: The Friedman-Komogortsev Method (FKM) is a rule-based classifier of fixations, saccades, and post-saccadic oscillations in 1000-Hz recordings, developed from the modified Nyström-Holmqvist algorithm (MNH) and used in several recent studies. FKM changes MNH in many ways at once: it centres MNH's Savitzky-Golay filter, adds a position-based test for whether an apparent post-saccadic oscillation continues the saccade, adds rejection tests, and changes several thresholds. We asked which of these changes alter agreement with human classification. Both algorithms were scored against twenty 26-s GazeBase reading recordings hand-classified by three trained raters, and each change was reverted in turn. FKM agreed better than MNH as MNH was used: saccade Cohen's kappa rose on all 20 recordings (median +0.034), and saccade boundaries moved from 2-3 ms late to the raters' sample. One change produced this: centring the filter, which removes a three-sample delay. Reinstating the delay returned FKM's saccade kappa to MNH's value, and centring MNH's filter alone made MNH match FKM on saccades and exceed it on post-saccadic events. The position-based test changed how saccades with several velocity peaks were divided, splitting 8% of rater-labelled "wavy" saccades into a saccade and a spurious oscillation against 39% for delay-corrected MNH. FKM's higher post-saccadic velocity floor traded recall for precision. The remaining changes had no measurable effect on these recordings. FKM's improvement over MNH is therefore a filter-alignment correction that MNH users can apply directly, plus a segmentation rule for multi-peak saccades.
papers.comment: The details about the classification is described in the supplementary materials

papers.title: Learning Actionable Information Landscapes for Multimodal Active Sensing in Hawkmoths
papers.summary: Animals integrate information across sensory modalities to guide exploration, suggesting that they maintain internal estimates of where actions are expected to reduce uncertainty. However, how such action-conditioned information maps are learned from multimodal sensory experience remains unclear, as previous studies have been largely confined to unimodal sensing frameworks. We introduce a multimodal predictive-coding framework for learning uncertainty-reduction maps from visual and mechanosensory observations in hawkmoth flower interaction tasks. A variational generative model trained on simulated environments recovers modality-specific information landscapes over the action space, capturing how visual patterns, surface geometry, and mechanosensory cues shape the value of exploratory actions. These learned maps are consistent with several features of hawkmoth behavior, including nonzero tracking offsets, probing along visual patterns, and geometry-dependent exploration. Applying the model to behavioral data from flower tracking and nectary search, we find that natural trajectories tend to occupy regions of high uncertainty reduction in these learned maps. Building on these observations, we develop an uncertainty-gated lexicographic algorithm that switches between information gathering and reward exploitation based on perceptual uncertainty. In nectary search, uncertainty gating improves learning relative to exploit-only, $ε$-greedy, fixed-time, and uncertainty-calibrated non-lexicographic controls, with better generalization and robustness to sensory and curvature shifts. These results link information landscapes learned through generative modeling to biological sensing and embodied exploration.

papers.title: Perception, Not Reasoning, Limits Visual Theory of Mind
papers.summary: Vision-language models pass text-based false-belief probes at near-human levels but drop by over twenty percentage points on abstract panels the moment the same problem is conveyed visually. The consensus diagnosis is conceptual, prescribing new belief-reasoning modules. We argue the dominant bottleneck is perceptual: not what the model cannot reason about, but what it cannot see. We propose a five-condition dissociation protocol that holds the reasoning task constant while varying perceptual fidelity from visual only to text only, and quantify the result with the Perceptual Contribution Ratio, the share of the visual-to-text gap a given fidelity closes. We test this on two kinds of scenes: abstract 2D panels in the Heider--Simmel tradition, and naturalistic 3D game scenes from MuMA-ToM and MindPower. The evaluation covers seven VLMs and roughly 159,000 API calls. Ground-truth scaffolds substantially close the gap in every setting, and on the abstract panels and MuMA-ToM they match or exceed the text-only reasoning. Whereas scaffolds built by automatic parsers, including frontier VLMs, fail. The most common error in the visual-only condition is \emph{reality bias}, which accounts for 60\% of false-belief failures. Models report where an object actually is, not where an absent agent believes it is. This points to a perceptual front-end that fails to track which agents were present at each moment. Under the evaluated protocol, structured visual scene-state extraction, rather than belief inference, is the dominant bottleneck for visual ToM.

papers.title: NeuroHorizon: Long-Horizon Forecasting of Neural Population Activity with Hierarchical Memory
papers.summary: Long-horizon forecasting of neural population activity tests whether a model has captured dynamics that remain predictive well beyond the observed history. Prediction quality typically declines as the horizon grows, yet neither short-horizon accuracy nor teacher-forced evaluation, which supplies the true activity preceding each predicted step, reveals how well models sustain predictions from an initial history alone. We compare direct multi-step prediction and autoregressive rollout on spiking recordings across horizons and introduce NeuroHorizon, which pairs event-based spike encoding with a causal decoder for population firing rates. Its hierarchical prediction memory keeps recent predictions at full temporal resolution and compresses earlier ones into segment summaries, giving the decoder both local detail and longer-range context. Under teacher-forced training this memory holds ground-truth activity, whereas during rollout it holds the model's own predictions. To reduce this mismatch, we train with scheduled sampling, progressively exposing the decoder to its own predictions. From 500 ms of macaque motor-cortex activity, NeuroHorizon achieves the highest forward-prediction score among the evaluated autonomous models at all four horizons from 100 to 1000 ms, and its per-bin predictions remain above a mean-firing-rate baseline across nearly the full 1 s window. Complementary experiments on macaque sensorimotor and mouse multi-region recordings show that performance generally increases with model and data size, alongside improved prediction after cross-subject pretraining and fine-tuning. Together, these results clarify how forecasting performance changes across horizons and offer an effective approach to long-horizon forecasting of neural population activity.
papers.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Main Track). 25 pages, including references, appendices, and the NeurIPS paper checklist

papers.title: Pixels over Symbols: Sensory Realism Improves Behavioral Alignment in Models of Cognition
papers.summary: Computational models of cognition have traditionally relied on abstract symbolic inputs that approximate sensory experiences with simplified vector representations. This simplification reflects historical computational constraints and a long-held assumption that the details of sensory realism are incidental to the study of cognitive processes. Recent advances have enabled the development of sensory-realistic models capable of performing diverse cognitive tasks, yet whether sensory realism meaningfully shapes cognition has not been formally established. We address this gap through a large-scale empirical comparison of abstract and sensory-realistic neural network models trained on a battery of memory-dependent decision-making tasks. Our results show that sensory-realistic models mirror human behavioral response patterns significantly more than their abstract counterparts, though a substantial gap to human internal behavioral consistency remains even for the best tested models. By analyzing the internal dynamics of these systems, we find that the learned recurrent weights are not the main source of this divergence. In fact, frozen abstract-trained weights driven by sensory-realistic inputs recover the human consistency of sensory-realistic models. The resulting dynamics are also within the seed-to-seed variability of sensory-realistic models. Together, our findings argue that across a broad set of visual working-memory tasks, sensory realism accounts for a substantial portion of the model-human behavioral agreement, more than the choice of sequence architecture and comparable to the choice of vision encoder. These results suggest that findings obtained from abstract task models in neuroscience should be more carefully interpreted in light of their potential behavioral limitations.

papers.title: Path-dependent triage: Early judgments lead conversational AI chatbots to miss mental-health emergencies
papers.summary: People increasingly bring mental-health concerns to consumer AI chatbots. In these conversations, clinically relevant information rarely arrives all at once. Instead, it unfolds over multiple turns, often in response to the questions the chatbot asks. Recognizing risk therefore depends on how a chatbot integrates newly disclosed information (inference) and on the questions it asks on each turn to elicit this information (context-seeking). Here we evaluated the conversational triage performance of 13 frontier AI chatbots tasked with engaging in 10-turn conversations with simulated users. Simulated users were grounded in one of 112 structured mental-health case files, each with an associated clinician-validated urgency level, from routine care to emergency. Chatbots failed to recognize one in five mental-health emergencies (20.3%), nearly four times the failure rate when all relevant clinical details were presented in a single message (5.6%). This gap was not explained by missing information: by the final turn, decisive facts had almost always been disclosed, and simply re-presenting those same facts as a single message reduced emergency under-triage to 12.1%. The problem lay instead in how the conversation unfolded, a phenomenon we refer to as path dependence. Early triage dispositions increasingly anchored later ones, such that emergencies missed early were rarely recovered as evidence accumulated. Context-seeking narrowed onto a small number of stereotyped questioning trajectories, with chatbots perseverating more than human clinicians given the same transcripts. Because the chatbot's running judgment shaped what it asked next, these two biases were plausibly coupled across turns. These dynamics are invisible to single-turn benchmarks but measurable in multi-turn evaluation, and point to concrete mitigations for safer conversational triage in consumer health AI.

papers.title: A hair-thin implant opens the entire depth of the mouse brain to revisiting the same structures at subcellular resolution
papers.summary: Ultrathin multimode-fibre endoscopes provide minimally invasive access to subcellular structures throughout the depth of the mouse brain. Here we introduce a chronically implantable interface with a diameter of 144 μm, about the thickness of a human hair, that extends this capability to longitudinal imaging, enabling repeated access to the same fine structures over extended periods. The system supports weeks-long tracking of individual dendritic spines, allowing quantitative comparison of their dynamics and survival across dendritic compartments. We further demonstrate longitudinal intracellular calcium imaging during spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity in the same cells across days, as well as repeated measurements of blood flow in the same vessels across multiple brain regions. This chronic endomicroscopic platform provides stable, minimally invasive optical access for longitudinal subcellular-resolution imaging of brain structure, activity and blood flow across depth.
